name: Analogy & Odd-One-Out — Spot the Relationship
whatIsIt: Both puzzles are about finding the RELATIONSHIP. In an analogy (A : B :: C : ?), you find how A links to B, then apply the SAME link to C. In odd-one-out, every item shares a hidden property except one — you find the shared rule, and the item that breaks it is the odd one.
whyNeeded: Analogy and classification questions are everywhere in reasoning and vocabulary tests. They train you to name the exact relationship instead of relying on a vague 'feels similar'.
realLifeUses: Spotting the exception in a data set

vocabulary.meaning: A : B :: C : D — the pair C:D must share the SAME relationship as A:B.
The exact rule linking a pair (double, opposite, part-of, same category…).
The single item that does NOT share the rule the others share.
A group defined by a shared property (even numbers, fruits, squares…).

story.title: Name the Link, Then Reuse It
story.text: Teacher writes 2 : 4 :: 5 : ?. Sana says '7?' Teacher asks: 'What is the LINK from 2 to 4?' Sana: 'It doubles!' 'Then reuse the same link on 5.' '5 doubled is 10!' Next: 'Odd one out — 4, 9, 16, 20, 25.' Sana lists them: 4,9,16,25 are perfect squares, but 20 is not. '20 is the odd one!' The lesson: first NAME the rule, then apply or break it.
story.answerInStory: 10 (the link is 'double'), and 20 is the odd one (the rest are perfect squares).

visual.caption: Analogy: find the link (here 'double') from the first pair, then apply the SAME link to the second.

teachingGallery.title: First name the rule, then apply or break it
teachingGallery.note: Analogy: reuse the rule. Odd-one-out: find the rule the majority shares; the exception breaks it.

examples.caption: 4, 9, 16, 25 are squares; 20 is not — the odd one.
Odd one out: the item that doesn't fit the shared property.

standardMethod.summary: State the relationship in words. For analogy, apply that same relationship to the new item. For odd-one-out, keep the item that does NOT obey the shared rule.
steps: Look at the given pair (or the whole set) and describe the link in a short phrase.
Check the link is exact — 'doubles', 'opposite', 'is a square', 'same category'.
For analogy: apply the identical link to the new term to get the answer.
For odd-one-out: the answer is the single item that breaks the shared rule.

alternateMethods.name: Try the obvious categories
alternateMethods.whenToUse: When you can't spot the rule quickly.
steps: Run a mental checklist: even/odd, squares/cubes, primes, same first letter, same group (fruits, metals).
The first checklist item that splits the set 'all-but-one' is your rule.
alternateMethods.example: 3, 5, 7, 9, 11 → all odd, but is one non-prime? 9 is not prime → odd one 9.

steps: Link from 3 to 9: it is 3 squared (3 × 3).
100 is not a perfect cube (it is 10²).

trickPractice.trick: Say the rule in one short phrase first
trickPractice.intro: If you can name the link, the answer is easy.

commonMistakes.mistake: Choosing an answer that 'feels related' without naming the exact rule.
commonMistakes.fix: Force yourself to say the link in words ('doubles', 'is a square'). A precise rule gives one clear answer; a vague feeling gives wrong ones.

commonMistakes.mistake: In odd-one-out, picking an item that DOES fit the rule instead of the exception.
commonMistakes.fix: Find the property the MAJORITY shares; the answer is the one that breaks it, not one that follows it.

teachBackPrompt: Explain to a friend how to solve 2 : 4 :: 5 : ? by naming the link ('double') and reusing it → 10. Then show odd-one-out of 4, 9, 16, 20, 25 → 20, because the others are perfect squares.

revisionCard.summary: Analogy & odd-one-out are both about the RELATIONSHIP. Analogy A:B::C:? — name the exact link from A to B, apply it to C. Odd-one-out — find the property the majority share (even, square, cube, prime, same category); the answer is the one that breaks it. Always state the rule in words first.

gameMission.title: Spot the Odd Beast
gameMission.brief: Name the hidden link and either complete the pair or catch the creature that doesn't belong! Precise rules win; vague guesses lose.

realLifeProject: Make a 'which one doesn't belong?' card with five items (four sharing a rule, one breaking it). Test three friends — a good card makes them explain the exact rule.

rememberIt.hook: Name the rule, then apply it or break it
rememberIt.unpack: Analogy reuses the link; odd-one-out keeps the item that breaks the shared rule.

studentQuestions.q: What if two answers seem to fit the analogy?
studentQuestions.a: Your rule is too loose. Tighten it — 'doubles' and 'adds 2' both fit 2→4, so check the second pair to decide which rule the question really means.

studentQuestions.q: How do I get faster at odd-one-out?
studentQuestions.a: Run a quick checklist: even/odd, squares, cubes, primes, same category. The first property that splits the set 'all-but-one' is your rule.
